title: The infrastructure files are generated and the image they describe actually serves health
description:
SPIDR child 1 of task-5d30948435524c6fa2789e1c033aafe7 (architect-20a6d1eb, 2026-09-05). Dependency-free LEAF.

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS: generating the infrastructure files from the approved contract's deployment requirements when the repository lacks them - a multi-stage Dockerfile for the controlled profile, a docker-compose with app + postgres, and a healthcheck - landed through the lander. Plus the proof that the image built from them ACTUALLY ANSWERS its health URL. No command kinds, no deploy effect, no UI.

MEASURED AT HEAD (branch moe/work-2026-09-04) by architect-20a6d1eb: no deployment surface exists at all; `grep -c deploy apps/daemon/src/daemon-command-vocabulary.ts` = 0 and there is no Dockerfile or compose file in the repo root. The gap is real.

A GENERATED DOCKERFILE THAT WAS NEVER BUILT IS A TEXT FILE. The parent's DoD 2 is explicit: the generated image BUILDS and ANSWERS its health URL, in a test that runs docker when present and otherwise fails with an explicit DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE line quoted in the step note - NEVER a silent pass. A golden test over the file bytes alone would ship a Dockerfile that cannot build, and the failure would surface at someone's first deploy.

COORDINATION with two sibling parents, neither expressible as dependsOn (the rail forbids sibling deps): the SCAFFOLD (task-4a0f706437a042059789be2ebdb98bc0) already emits a docker-compose with postgres per the controlled profile - so decide and record whether this row GENERATES infrastructure only when the repository lacks it (the parent's wording) or whether the scaffold's compose is the one it extends. Duplicating compose files is how a product ends up with two postgres services. The MIGRATIONS row (task-8f86e10504c74e248ccfa6f427b41a15) assumes a compose with postgres too.
definitionOfDone: A golden test pins the generated Dockerfile, docker-compose and healthcheck bytes for the controlled profile, generated from the approved contract's deployment requirements. Two generations with the same contract are byte-identical.

GENERATION IS CONDITIONAL AND NON-DESTRUCTIVE: files are generated only when the repository LACKS them, and an existing Dockerfile or compose is never overwritten. Assert that a repository already carrying one keeps its own bytes - a generator that clobbers an operator's infrastructure is the worst outcome here.

THE IMAGE BUILDS AND SERVES HEALTH: a test builds the image and probes the healthcheck until it answers, on a machine with docker. Assert the health response, not merely a successful build - an image that builds and crashes on start passes a build-only test.

DOCKER ABSENT FAILS LOUDLY: with no docker the test refuses with an explicit DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE line quoted in the step note, never a silent pass or a skip. Say plainly in the completion record whether the build arm actually RAN on the machine that produced the gate output.

The relationship to the scaffold's own compose is decided and RECORDED: either this row generates only what is missing (leaving the scaffold's compose authoritative) or it extends it - state which, and assert no product ends up with two postgres services. The migrations row assumes one compose with postgres.
Gates quoted with their `Test Files N passed` count lines: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`.
taskRails: NEVER OVERWRITE EXISTING INFRASTRUCTURE. Generate only what the repository lacks; an operator's Dockerfile is theirs.
BUILD THE IMAGE AND PROBE IT. A byte-golden test on a Dockerfile proves formatting, not that it works.
DOCKER ABSENT IS A LOUD FAILURE, never a skip — and the record must say whether the build arm ran.
ONE COMPOSE, ONE POSTGRES. Coordinate with the scaffold row (task-4a0f7064) and the migrations row (task-8f86e105); duplicating services is how a product gets two databases.
NO COMMAND KINDS, NO DEPLOY EFFECT, NO UI: those are children 2 and 3.

implementationPlan.description: MEASUREMENT + THE RECORDED RULING (DoD 5). Re-measured at HEAD of moe/work-2026-09-04, not from the description. (a) The scaffold row task-4a0f7064 LANDED at 2feed27b and ALREADY emits `docker-compose.yml` carrying exactly ONE postgres service `db` (postgres:17-alpine, pg_isready healthcheck, db-data volume) — `controlled-profile-root-templates.ts:124-208`. (b) It emits NO Dockerfile, NO .dockerignore, NO app service. (c) The generated api already serves `GET /health` -> 200 `{"status":"ok"}` on `PORT` (default 3000) and binds only as process entry point — `controlled-profile-package-templates.ts:170-211`. (d) `packages/api` has NO runtime dependencies, only devDependencies, so the runtime stage needs node + dist only. (e) `deploymentRequirements` EXISTS on the v2 contract revision (`packages/core/src/product-contract/product-contract-v2-contract.ts:154`) but its elements are PROSE statements (`ProductContractV2Requirement` = statement/requirementId/priority/dependsOn), carrying no port or health-path fields. THE RULING, recorded here and posted as a task comment: this row GENERATES ONLY WHAT THE REPOSITORY LACKS. The scaffold's `docker-compose.yml` stays authoritative and is NEVER rewritten; the app service ships as `docker-compose.override.yml`, which docker compose merges into the base file by default — ONE project, ONE postgres service (`db`), which is exactly what the migrations row task-8f86e105 assumes. Because the requirements are prose, they are NOT parsed into build parameters (that would be fabricated authority); they are carried as a sorted PROVENANCE list of requirementIds in the emitted headers, so the contract is genuinely load-bearing on the bytes and determinism is testable over it.
implementationPlan.note:

implementationPlan.description: Write `deployment-infrastructure-templates.ts`: the byte templates, same determinism discipline as the scaffold sibling (line arrays joined with \n plus trailing \n, never a multi-line template literal, no clock/random/cwd/os.EOL). Four artifacts. (1) `Dockerfile` — multi-stage: `FROM node:24.16.0-alpine AS build` (version pinned to match the profile's `engines.node` and its CI workflow), corepack enable, COPY tree, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm --filter api build`; then `FROM node:24.16.0-alpine AS runtime`, copy ONLY `packages/api/dist` plus the healthcheck, `ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000`, `EXPOSE 3000`, `HEALTHCHECK` exec-form, `USER node`, `CMD ["node","/app/dist/server.js"]`. (2) `.dockerignore` — node_modules, dist, .env, logs, playwright output; without it `COPY . .` would ship the host's node_modules into the build context. (3) `docker-compose.override.yml` — ONLY an `app` service (build ., ports 3000, `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy`, environment read from the env, its own healthcheck). NO postgres service and NO `volumes:` key: both come from the base file. (4) `docker/healthcheck.mjs` — a node HTTP GET of /health asserting status 200, so the check depends on no tool outside the image. EPIC RAIL 3: no credential literal in any emitted byte — every value is `${VAR}` or read from the environment, mirroring the scaffold's own comment. Plus its `.js` bridge (the package convention: `.ts` files import `./x.js` and `node --experimental-strip-types` does not rewrite the extension).
implementationPlan.note:
Templates written, 193 lines (per-file cap 250 target / 400 hard — under both). The four artifacts and the reasoning that is load-bearing on later steps:

1. `Dockerfile` — two stages on `node:24.16.0-alpine`, pinned to the profile's own `engines.node` (">=24.16.0 <25") and to the node version its CI workflow sets up; a floating `node:24-alpine` would make two builds of the same contract differ, which DoD 1 forbids. Build stage: corepack enable, `COPY . .`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm --filter api build`. Runtime stage copies ONLY `packages/api/dist` plus the healthcheck — measured in step 1, `packages/api` declares devDependencies only, so no `node_modules` is needed at runtime at all. HEALTHCHECK and CMD are both exec form, so the signal reaching PID 1 is the one docker sent.

2. `.dockerignore` — the one that matters is `.env`: without it `COPY . .` bakes a real credential into an image layer, which is epic rail 3 breached in the worst possible way (layers survive deletion of the file). Also excludes node_modules and dist so the host's platform-specific binaries never enter the context.

3. `docker-compose.override.yml` — ONLY the `app` service, per the step-1 ruling. No `db`, no `volumes:` key. `docker compose` merges this into the scaffold's `docker-compose.yml` by default, so `db`, its pg_isready healthcheck and the `db-data` volume come from the base file and are not restated. `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy` is what makes the merge load-bearing rather than decorative.

4. `docker/healthcheck.mjs` — a node HTTP GET rather than curl/wget. The runtime image's shell tools are busybox applets that can change between base image revisions; probing with the runtime that is definitionally present makes the check depend on nothing the image lacks. It exits 0 ONLY on a 200 — timeout, transport error and any other status exit 1, because a check that exits 0 on connection-refused reports a dead app as healthy.

EPIC RAIL 3 HELD: no credential literal in any emitted byte. `DATABASE_URL` uses `${DATABASE_URL:?set DATABASE_URL in .env}` — the compose-native required-variable form, so a missing value is a loud refusal rather than a silent empty string. Step 5 asserts this with a test arm rather than leaving it as a claim.

DETERMINISM DISCIPLINE: line arrays joined with "\n" plus one trailing "\n", never a multi-line template literal (whose indentation would follow this source file's formatting), no clock/random/cwd/os.EOL. The port, health path, entry path, healthcheck path and base image are exported consts so the tests in step 5 can compare the Dockerfile against the scaffold's api template instead of restating literals.

Plus the tracked one-line `.js` bridge, matching the sibling convention verified in step 1.

implementationPlan.description: Write `deployment-infrastructure-generator.ts`: the conditional, non-destructive generation decision as a PURE function over (profileVersion, deploymentRequirements, the set of paths the repository already carries). Returns a discriminated result: `{ok:true, write: ReadonlyMap<path,bytes>, kept: readonly path[]}` or `{ok:false, code}`. Stable refusal codes, exported as consts in the sibling's style: `DEPLOY_PROFILE_VERSION_UNKNOWN` (asked for a profile this build cannot emit) and `DEPLOY_REQUIREMENTS_ABSENT` (the contract carries zero deployment requirements — DoD 1 says the files are generated FROM them, so generating with none would be inventing them). NON-DESTRUCTIVE IS STRUCTURAL, NOT A FLAG: a path present in the existing-path set never appears in `write`, it appears in `kept` — the caller is handed no bytes it could clobber with. Requirement ids are sorted by UTF-16 code unit before they reach the provenance header, so two generations from the same contract are byte-identical regardless of the order the contract lists them. Plus its `.js` bridge.
implementationPlan.note:
Generator written, 106 lines. `planDeploymentInfrastructure(request)` is pure: inputs are the profile version, the approved contract's `deploymentRequirements`, and the set of paths the repository already carries.

NON-DESTRUCTIVE IS STRUCTURAL, NOT A FLAG (DoD 2, task rail 1). A path already in the repository never appears in `write`; it appears in `kept`, and its BYTES are absent from the result entirely. The generator never reads or reproduces an operator's file, so there is no overwrite branch to get wrong, no `force` option a caller could pass, and no way to round-trip someone's Dockerfile back at them subtly changed. Step 5 asserts the operator's foreign bytes SURVIVING, not merely that a boolean flipped.

REFUSAL CODES, per global rail 1 (assert the reason code, not the outcome). Both exported as consts in the sibling generator's style:
- `DEPLOY_PROFILE_VERSION_UNKNOWN` — the request names a profile this build cannot emit. Compared against `CONTROLLED_PROFILE_VERSION` imported from the scaffold generator, so the two cannot drift apart into a version this row thinks it supports and the scaffold does not.
- `DEPLOY_REQUIREMENTS_ABSENT` — the contract carries zero deployment requirements. DoD 1 says the files are generated FROM them; emitting infrastructure that satisfies nothing would invent the requirement, and the provenance header would name an empty set while claiming to trace.

DETERMINISM OVER THE CONTRACT (DoD 1). `orderedRequirementIds` de-duplicates through a Set and sorts by UTF-16 code unit before the ids reach any header, so a contract listing the same requirements in a different order yields byte-identical files, and two rows naming one requirement id do not double it. Step 5's shuffled-input arm is what proves the sort rather than merely the absence of a clock — deleting the `.sort()` must red it, and step 8 verifies that by mutation.

DEPENDENCY EDGE VERIFIED, not assumed (global rail 7). This module imports `ProductContractV2Requirement` from the BARE specifier `@moe/core`. Measured: `apps/daemon/package.json` declares `"@moe/core": "workspace:*"` in dependencies, `packages/core/src/index.ts:169` exports the type from the root barrel, and `apps/daemon/src` already carries real bare-specifier `from "@moe/core"` imports (e.g. activation-world-fixtures.ts:37) — so the importer edge is live, not one this row would have to add. It is an `import type`, so it erases at runtime and adds no value import.

Plus the tracked one-line `.js` bridge.

implementationPlan.description: Write `deployment-docker-probe.ts`: the docker availability probe as a seam separate from the test, so its reason code is assertable without docker. `spawnSync` with an argv array and `shell:false`, executable `docker` (never a hard-coded path — global rail on host-executable launchers), running `docker version --format {{.Server.Version}}`; returns `{available:true, serverVersion}` or `{available:false, code: DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE, detail}`. THE CLI EXISTING IS NOT THE DAEMON RUNNING — measured on this host, `docker version` prints `failed to connect to the docker API at npipe:...` while the CLI resolves fine, so the probe must classify on the SERVER version being parseable, not on the binary being found or on exit status alone. Exports `DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE` as a const. Plus its `.js` bridge.
implementationPlan.note:
Docker probe written, 93 lines, and RUN against this host rather than reasoned about.

SPLIT INTO TWO PIECES ON PURPOSE. `classifyDockerProbe(outcome)` is a pure function of the spawn's result; `probeDocker()` does the spawn and hands its result to it. That is what makes DoD 4's refusal code assertable in the always-on lane on a machine with no docker at all — step 5/6 feed the classifier synthetic outcomes (ENOENT, daemon-down, a live version) and pin the code, instead of the reason code being reachable only on a host that already has what the test is checking for.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS A PARSEABLE SERVER VERSION ON STDOUT, not "the binary was found" and not the exit status. Both alternatives are wrong here and I measured why:
- `command -v docker` -> `/c/Program Files/Docker/Docker/resources/bin/docker`. The CLI is installed. Classifying on that would call this host docker-capable and the failure would resurface later as an unreadable build error.
- Exit status is unreliable through a pipe — my first probe read `exit=0` because `$?` was `head`'s status, not docker's. Running the probe directly shows docker itself exits 1. A seam that trusts the status of a piped command is a false green waiting to happen.
Only a live daemon can put a `major.minor` version on stdout, so that is the test.

VERIFIED ON THIS HOST, output verbatim:
  {"available":false,"code":"DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE","detail":"no docker daemon answered (exit 1): failed to connect to the docker API at npipe:////./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine; check if the path is correct and if the daemon is running: open //./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine: The system cannot find the file specified."}
  DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE: no docker daemon answered (exit 1): failed to connect to the docker API at npipe:////./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine; check if the path is correct and if the daemon is running: open //./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine: The system cannot find the file specified.
Command: `node --experimental-strip-types -e "import('./src/repository/deployment/deployment-docker-probe.ts')..."` from apps/daemon. So: DOCKER CLI PRESENT, DAEMON DOWN on this machine — the build arm will NOT run here, and step 7 records that plainly rather than dressing it up.

HOST-EXECUTABLE LAUNCHER RAIL HELD: executable `docker`, argv array, `shell:false`, 20 s timeout. Never a hard-coded absolute path (it differs per host) and never a command string — a shell would re-parse the `{{.Server.Version}}` braces. `dockerUnavailableLine()` produces the quoted line in ONE place, so the completion record quotes what the code emits rather than a paraphrase of it.

implementationPlan.description: Write `deployment-infrastructure-generator.test.ts` — ALWAYS-ON arms, all four DoD clauses that do not need docker. (1) GOLDEN BYTES (DoD 1): pin the full text of all four artifacts as expected literals, asserted with toEqual against the generated map. (2) DETERMINISM (DoD 1): two generations from the same contract are byte-identical, INCLUDING one whose requirement list is shuffled — proving the sort, not just the absence of a clock. (3) NON-DESTRUCTIVE (DoD 2): a repository already carrying a `Dockerfile` and a `docker-compose.override.yml` with distinctive foreign bytes gets those paths in `kept` and ABSENT from `write`, and the assertion is on the FOREIGN BYTES SURVIVING, not merely on a boolean. (4) REFUSAL CODES, per global rail 1 — assert the specific code `DEPLOY_PROFILE_VERSION_UNKNOWN` and `DEPLOY_REQUIREMENTS_ABSENT`, never merely that it refused. (5) ONE COMPOSE, ONE POSTGRES (DoD 5, rail 4): parse the scaffold's real base compose via `controlledProfileRootFiles` — the actual producer, not a copy — merge the emitted override's service keys over it, and assert exactly ONE service whose image is a `postgres:` image and exactly one service named `db`. This arm reds the day anyone adds a second database to either file. (6) PRECONDITIONS THE BUILD ARM DEPENDS ON, so the opt-in arm can never be vacuous: the Dockerfile's runtime CMD path equals the api package's `start` script target, the exposed port equals the api template's PORT default, and the healthcheck path equals the route the api template answers 200 on — each read out of the scaffold templates, not restated as a literal. (7) EPIC RAIL 3: assert no emitted byte matches the profile's own `CHANGE_ME` placeholder or a `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=` literal value.
implementationPlan.note:
Always-on arms written and GREEN. 9 tests, no docker needed for any of them.

  npx vitest run --root . --config package.json --testTimeout=30000 src/repository/deployment/deployment-infrastructure-generator.test.ts
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
  Tests  9 passed (9)   Duration 1.65s

(run from apps/daemon. The `--root . --config package.json` shape is the daemon's own — vitest's root config does not reach apps/**.)

The arms, and what each would have to be to be vacuous:
1. GOLDEN BYTES (DoD 1) — all four artifacts pinned in full, plus the exact KEY LIST, so adding or dropping a generated file reds. Plus no `\r` in any emitted byte.
2. DETERMINISM OVER THE CONTRACT (DoD 1) — the fixture deliberately lists the two requirements OUT of sorted order, and separate arms reverse the list and duplicate an id. All three must produce identical maps. This proves the sort and the de-duplication, not merely the absence of a clock; step 8 mutates the `.sort()` away to confirm it reds.
3. THE CONTRACT IS LOAD-BEARING — a different requirement set produces DIFFERENT Dockerfile bytes carrying the new id. Without this arm the provenance could be dropped entirely and every other arm would stay green, which is exactly how a "generated from the contract" claim becomes decoration.
4. NON-DESTRUCTIVE (DoD 2) — the assertion is on the OPERATOR'S BYTES SURVIVING: a hand-written `FROM scratch` Dockerfile is put on a simulated disk, the plan's writes are applied over it, and the operator's bytes must still be there. It also asserts what the repository LACKS is still generated (`.dockerignore`, `docker/healthcheck.mjs`), so "non-destructive" cannot be satisfied by generating nothing.
5+6. REFUSAL CODES, per global rail 1 — the SPECIFIC codes `DEPLOY_PROFILE_VERSION_UNKNOWN` and `DEPLOY_REQUIREMENTS_ABSENT`, never merely `ok === false`.
7. ONE COMPOSE, ONE POSTGRES (DoD 5, task rail 4) — reads the scaffold's REAL base compose via `controlledProfileRootFiles`, the producer itself and not a copy pasted into the test, merges the override's services over it, and asserts merged service names are exactly [app, db] and that exactly ONE service carries a `postgres:` image, named `db`. Also that the override contributes no postgres and no volumes block. This reds the day anyone adds a second database to either file — which is the failure task rail 4 names. The compose reader is a ~20-line reader for THESE TWO FILES, not a YAML implementation; both are generated with fixed two-space service indentation, and there is no yaml parser anywhere in this repo (`git grep '"yaml"\|"js-yaml"' -- '**/package.json'` -> no hits), so adding a dependency for two known-shape files would be the larger risk.
8. PRECONDITIONS THE BUILD ARM DEPENDS ON — the api's `start` script target, the api's PORT default and the route it answers 200 on are all extracted FROM THE SCAFFOLD TEMPLATES and compared to the Dockerfile and healthcheck. This is what keeps the golden honest on a host where the image cannot be built: a Dockerfile pointing at a path the api does not emit reds here, with no docker involved.
9. EPIC RAIL 3, NO SECRET IN ANY EMITTED BYTE — the placeholder is read out of the profile's own `.env.example` rather than restated, then asserted absent from every emitted file, plus a regex for any PASSWORD/SECRET/TOKEN assignment whose value is not a `${...}` reference. And `.dockerignore` must exclude `.env`: an image layer outlives the file, so a credential that reaches the build context is not recoverable by deleting it.

ONE PROCESS NOTE for whoever runs these next: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test src/repository/deployment` does NOT narrow to that directory — it ran the whole daemon suite past 300 s. Use the direct vitest invocation above to scope to a file.

implementationPlan.description: Write `deployment-image-build.test.ts` — the arm that makes DoD 3 real, modelled on the sibling `controlled-profile-build.test.ts` precedent. OPT-IN via `MOE_DEPLOY_IMAGE_BUILD=1`, for the reason the sibling records verbatim: unconditionally it would run inside `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, the gate EVERY row on this board runs, and would red on any host without docker — making every later gate inadmissible. THE OPT-IN IS NOT A SKIP (DoD 4, task rail 3): when the flag IS set and docker is unavailable the arm FAILS LOUDLY with the exact line `DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE: ...`, never a skip and never a silent pass. An ALWAYS-ON arm asserts that refusal wiring itself against the probe seam, so the loud-failure path is covered on this docker-less host too. The expensive arm: write the scaffold tree plus the generated infrastructure to a temp dir, `docker build` a UNIQUELY TAGGED image, `docker run -d` publishing a port, then POLL the health URL until it answers and assert the RESPONSE — status 200 and body `{"status":"ok"}` — because an image that builds and crashes on start passes a build-only test. EPIC RAIL 4, ANYTHING THIS EPIC STARTS IT STOPS: `docker rm -f` the container and `docker rmi -f` the image and rm the temp dir in a `finally`, on the throwing path too — a leaked container makes every later gate on this board inadmissible. Separate foreground legs, argv arrays, shell:false, no `&&` chain (reports only the last status) and no pipe.
implementationPlan.note:
Image-build arm written, and BOTH of its states run and quoted. 219 lines.

STATE 1 — flag absent, the state every other row on this board sees:
  npx vitest run --root . --config package.json --testTimeout=30000 src/repository/deployment/deployment-image-build.test.ts
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
  Tests  2 passed | 1 skipped (3)

STATE 2 — THE DoD 4 PROOF. Flag set, docker daemon down on this host. The arm was asked to run and refused LOUDLY, verbatim:

  MOE_DEPLOY_IMAGE_BUILD=1 npx vitest run --root . --config package.json --testTimeout=60000 src/repository/deployment/deployment-image-build.test.ts

  FAIL  src/repository/deployment/deployment-image-build.test.ts > the generated image > builds from the generated Dockerfile and answers its health URL
  AssertionError: DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE: no docker daemon answered (exit 1): failed to connect to the docker API at npipe:////./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine; check if the path is correct and if the daemon is running: open //./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine: The system cannot find the file specified.
  Test Files  1 failed (1)
  Tests  1 failed | 2 passed (3)

SAY IT PLAINLY, as DoD 4 demands: THE BUILD ARM DID NOT RUN on this machine. Docker Desktop's CLI is installed; its daemon is not running. Nothing in this row has ever built an image or answered a health URL on this host. What IS proven here is that asking for the build on a docker-less host produces a named, loud failure instead of a green — the failure mode the DoD calls out.

THE TWO CONDITIONS ARE KEPT SEPARATE, which is the whole design: without the FLAG the expensive arm does not run (the scaffold sibling's precedent — unconditionally it would execute inside `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, the gate every row runs, and red on any offline host, making every later gate on this board inadmissible). With the flag set and NO DOCKER it fails loudly. "Skip" is never the answer to docker being absent.

TWO ALWAYS-ON ARMS keep that refusal from being reachable only where it cannot be tested:
- The classifier is pinned on three synthetic outcomes — daemon-down (stderr npipe, exit 1), not-installed (ENOENT), and a live server version — asserting the specific code `DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE`, not merely "unavailable". The daemon-down case is the one that matters: a binary-presence check calls that host capable and the build then fails somewhere far less legible.
- The refusal LINE format is pinned against the same `dockerUnavailableLine` the arm calls, so this note quotes what the code emits.

WHAT THE EXPENSIVE ARM DOES WHEN A HOST HAS DOCKER: materializes the scaffold tree plus this row's generated infrastructure into a temp dir (note `existingPaths: scaffold.files.keys()` — the generator is handed the scaffold's real path set, so the same non-destructive rule that protects an operator is what runs here); `docker build`; `docker run --detach` publishing an OS-assigned free port bound to 127.0.0.1; then POLLS until the health URL ANSWERS and asserts status 200 AND body `{"status":"ok"}` — DoD 3's point being that an image which builds and crashes on start passes a build-only test.

ADVERSARIAL PASS RUN AS DRILLS, NOT AS READING. Five mutations of the production surface; each had to red a NAMED arm. Two of them found real defects, both now fixed.

M1 — delete `.sort()` in orderedRequirementIds -> RED: golden bytes + "byte-identical whatever order it lists the requirements in". (2 failed / 9 passed)
M2 — inject a second postgres service (`db2: image: postgres:17-alpine`) into the override -> RED: golden + "leaves the product with one compose project and exactly one postgres service". This is task rail 4's exact failure and the arm catches it. (2 failed / 9 passed)

M4/M5 — rewrite the generated healthcheck to `process.exit(0)` -> see the two findings below.

FINDING 1 (real, in my own new arm — found by drilling it). M5 first showed the healthcheck mutation reddening ONLY the byte-golden arm: the executable arm still passed, because its two cases were "app answers 200" and "nothing is listening". A script hard-wired to `process.exit(0)` passes the first, and the second is caught by the `error` handler the mutation never touched. So the arm asserted the reachable-and-healthy and the unreachable cases and was blind to the one that matters: REACHABLE BUT UNHEALTHY. Added a 503 case with a server whose answer varies, and re-drilled:
  M5 REDRILL -> RED on BOTH "pins the bytes..." and "runs the healthcheck it generates: 0 only when the app answers 200" (2 failed / 10 passed).
That is the arm earning its place. Without it, the healthcheck's SEMANTICS were pinned only as text, and on a host with no docker nothing would have noticed a check that reports every dead container healthy.

FINDING 2 (real, in production bytes). While debugging the new arm I measured that the generated script's socket deadline was 2000 ms while the Dockerfile's `HEALTHCHECK --timeout` was 5s. An inner deadline SHORTER than docker's outer one means an app answering at 3 s is called unhealthy and its container restarted, before docker had decided to give up on it. Fixed by deriving both from one exported constant, `DEPLOYMENT_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5`, so they cannot drift; the golden literal was updated with it.

A THIRD THING THE DRILL CAUGHT, in the test only, worth recording because it looked exactly like a product bug: the first version of the arm used `spawnSync`, which BLOCKS this process's event loop — so the in-process server could never accept the child's connection and the check "timed out" against a server that was fine. The control that settled it: raising the socket timeout 2000 -> 15000 moved the failure from 2016 ms to 15016 ms (never connecting), while an in-process request to the same server answered in 0-6 ms. Cause was the harness, not the script. The arm now uses async `spawn`, and the comment says why so nobody re-introduces it.
